acquisition.why: Gym owners are often sole traders, so cold email and DMs to them are restricted. That leaves Meta ads, SEO and a free tier, all expensive and slow in a crowded category [E].

onboarding.why: Migrating members, payments and access hardware usually needs a hand-held setup (hence the $700 fee). Agents can script most of it.

delivery.why: It is software, but bookings, payments and door integrations need ongoing upkeep and uptime responsibility.

billing.why: Stripe subscriptions plus processing run unattended.

support.why: Gyms depend on it every day; failed check-ins and payment issues need fast human support.

scores.R_why: A full gym platform with payments, check-in hardware and a CRM is far beyond 6-8 h/week and £300. Ricardo would also carry payment-facilitator compliance and uptime liability.
scores.M_why: The UK is saturated (Glofox, TeamUp, Mindbody, Gymdesk, PushPress). Switching costs are high and differentiation is low.
scores.one_line: The revenue figures are host guesses about a funded incumbent, and a niche wedge (e.g. a check-in add-on) is the only conceivable angle; poor fit for an agent-run part-timer [E].

acquisition.why: Organic TikTok and Instagram, Etsy and paid ads are all inbound and legal. Agents can produce content, but brand building needs taste and steady posting, and it depends on platforms.

onboarding.why: Shoppers buy through the checkout; nothing to onboard.

delivery.why: The POD supplier fulfils each order. Physical goods still need QC, sample checks and handling of shipping issues, which caps it a little.

billing.why: Shopify or Etsy checkout runs unattended.

support.why: Sizing, returns and delays are routine tickets an agent can handle with escalation. UK 14-day returns rules apply.

scores.R_why: £300 covers samples and a store. However, overseas fulfilment adds UK VAT and import-duty friction, and premium pricing needs brand credibility that is hard to build in a few hours a week.
scores.M_why: Apparel and POD are extremely saturated, ad costs are high, and AI makes lookalike brands trivial to launch.
scores.one_line: The pipeline automates easily, but the source is sponsored supplier content with no sales proof, in the most crowded consumer category [E].

acquisition.why: UK trades are mostly sole traders, so the scrape-and-text method shown is illegal under PECR. Cold email works only to Ltd firms (findable via Companies House), plus SEO and template marketplaces [E].

onboarding.why: Each business needs its pricing logic configured. An agent can collect inputs through a form, but a human should check the quote logic.

delivery.why: An embedded widget runs unattended once the logic is right.

billing.why: Paddle or Stripe subscriptions; Paddle also handles VAT.

support.why: Requests to adjust pricing and complaints about bad quotes are routine for an agent.

scores.R_why: Technical Ricardo can build this cheaply. The hard parts are getting customers legally and the low willingness to pay of small UK trades.
scores.M_why: Easy to copy, and quote features are already in Jobber, Tradify, ServiceM8 and form builders. Niche-vertical SEO has some room.
scores.one_line: A cheap, automatable micro-SaaS, but a commoditised feature with a hard legal acquisition path to UK sole-trader trades [E].

acquisition.why: No channel was given. SEO or Product Hunt for a single-purpose tool is possible but unproven.

delivery.why: Workflows run unattended, but scrapers break and need maintenance.

scores.R_why: This is a technique, not a business, and it is easy for Ricardo. The scraping example raises terms-of-service risk and low willingness to pay.
scores.M_why: Consumer AI agents and existing alert tools (e.g. Honey, Keepa-style) replace thin workflow wrappers [E].
scores.one_line: Illustrative only, with no customer, price or evidence; viable only if paired with a validated niche need [E].

acquisition.why: App Store search and content are legal inbound channels, but the category is very crowded and visibility usually needs paid UA.

support.why: Data-loss and sync complaints, plus GDPR requests, are routine for an agent.

scores.R_why: Buildable within the budget. Mood and health journaling data under UK GDPR and sending it to AI providers need care, and monetising takes long ASO grinding.
scores.M_why: Day One, Reflectly, Stoic, Rosebud and the built-in Apple Journal crowd the space, and AI makes clones trivial.
scores.one_line: Fully automatable, but a tutorial demo in a saturated category with no revenue evidence [E].

acquisition.why: Cold email to UK limited companies is legal and fits the service itself, and agents can run it with compliance screening of who is contacted.

onboarding.why: Each client needs ICP definition, account access and approval of messaging.

delivery.why: Agents do the enrichment and drafting, with human QA on accuracy and sender reputation.

support.why: Clients expect reporting and someone accountable for results.

scores.R_why: Skills fit well, but this is service work with client accountability that strains 6-8 h/week. Ricardo would carry PECR and GDPR liability for each client's lists.
scores.M_why: Clay, Apollo and many lead-gen agencies crowd the space, and ChatGPT agents commoditise it. Vertical niches remain possible.
scores.one_line: Eight videos but mostly host musings with one trivial first-hand claim; legal B2B and automatable, but a commoditising, accountability-heavy service [E].

acquisition.why: SEO-led and legal, though it depends on Google and AI Overviews.

onboarding.why: Getting providers to pay for placements needs selling and verification.

delivery.why: Agents can maintain the directory data with periodic checks.

scores.R_why: The cited niches (Medicaid, rehab, paid plasma) don't translate to the UK. UK health-advertising rules (ASA, CQC) apply, and accuracy liability is high for an agent-run site.
scores.M_why: The UK has incumbents (BACP directory, Psychology Today, Doctify, NHS) and AI search is eroding directory traffic. Narrow UK niches may remain.
scores.one_line: An inbound, automatable model in principle, but the evidence is US-specific and health accuracy risk weakens a UK agent-run version [E].

acquisition.why: Camplify and Goboony marketplaces, legal inbound, but platform-dependent.

delivery.why: Physical work: handovers, cleaning, tank dumps and repairs.

support.why: Breakdowns and 3am calls need a human.

scores.R_why: Needs a £15-40k vehicle, storage and weekend turnovers, impossible on £300 and a toddler's schedule [E].
scores.M_why: UK campervan hire demand is decent, but the season is short and competition on the platforms is growing.
scores.one_line: Real first-hand evidence, but it is capital-heavy, physical and seasonal, the opposite of agent-run [E].
